extracted.intended_audience: marketers, brand managers, advertising/branding agency professionals and students of marketing
extracted.subtask_description: A short case-study style analysis of the New Coke failure that draws lessons for brand positioning and product-change decisions. Focuses on how perceptions, heritage, and competitive positioning govern consumer response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with core brand identity
rubrics_metrics.description: A brand can only stand for one cohesive idea; Coke undermined its own position by trying to be both the 'Real Thing' and the 'New Thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you tell the world you are the 'Real Thing,' then you can't come up with the 'New Real Thing.' Repositioning must not contradict long-held brand associations or core promise; do not attempt changes that are counter to the idea the brand owns in consumers' minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is stronger than reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception affects taste in the same way it affects all human judgment; perception is the reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective test results (e.g., blind taste tests) may show a product is 'better,' but if consumer perception or brand meaning disagrees, changes will fail. Marketing decisions should prioritize understanding and managing consumer perception, not just product attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning: battle of perceptions, not products
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing is a battle of perceptions, not products (Jack Trout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic positioning must focus on the perceptions the brand occupies relative to competitors; product improvements alone won't overcome entrenched perceptual positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach for a No.2 brand
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to position a No.2 in a category is to go against the No.1; Pepsi targeted youth with 'The Choice of a New Generation' to oppose Coke's 'the real thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you are second in a category, adopt a contrarian positioning that exploits weaknesses in the leader's implied audience (e.g., appeal to younger consumers if the leader is seen as for older people). Align messaging and creative to that differential position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of quantitative product testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Coca‑Cola ran a quarter-million taste tests and found a formula that beat Pepsi in blind tests, yet consumer backlash still occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative tests (blind taste tests) as important inputs but complement them with qualitative research into brand meaning, emotional associations, and consumer identity; don't let favorable test scores alone justify a change that conflicts with brand perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of brand heritage
rubrics_metrics.description: Heritage and origins can be central to a brand's meaning; Coke realized it is about heritage—the original, 'the real thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a brand's heritage is a core part of its positioning, product changes risk alienating loyal customers. Evaluate the role of heritage before altering iconic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of customer backlash when changing beloved products
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing a core product can provoke unrelenting backlash, revolt, boycotts, and massive consumer complaints (e.g., nearly 10,000 calls a day to Coke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate strong emotional reactions and build mitigation strategies (gradual changes, transparent communication, limited tests, opt-ins) before altering beloved products or retiring original versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment between advertising/messaging and brand identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to appear 'hip' or target new audiences must align with the brand's established identity; Coke's attempt to be 'new' conflicted with its 'original' identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure campaigns and creative executions are consistent with the brand's owned idea; trying to adopt opposing tones or promises will confuse consumers and weaken positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness and corrective action after failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Coca‑Cola quickly acknowledged its failure and brought back the original formula, which restored and increased sales and market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a strategic change provokes clear negative market response, act decisively to correct course; timely acknowledgement and reversal can limit damage and restore trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming product superiority guarantees market success
rubrics_metrics.description: To beat Pepsi in the marketplace, Coke thought a better-tasting cola would be enough, but product superiority didn't ensure acceptance because of brand meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume improvements in product metrics automatically translate to market acceptance; assess how product changes interact with brand promise and consumer identity before implementation.
